name: SwiftDrome
subtitle: A SwiftUI client for Navidrome and Subsonic-API music servers.
description:
SwiftDrome is an iOS client for Subsonic-API-compatible music servers (primarily Navidrome), built with SwiftUI and Apple's Liquid Glass design language.

Log in to your own Navidrome/Subsonic server and browse your library: artists, albums, playlists, genres, and search. Stream playback with a queue engine that keeps a user-controlled "Play Next" stack separate from the main queue, plus favorites and back-skip history.

This source publishes unsigned .ipa builds automatically whenever a change is released, so the version here should always track the latest build.

apps.localizedDescription:
SwiftDrome is an iOS client for Subsonic-API-compatible music servers (primarily Navidrome), built with SwiftUI and Apple's Liquid Glass design language.

Log in to your own Navidrome/Subsonic server and browse your library: artists, albums, playlists, genres, and search. Stream playback with a queue engine that keeps a user-controlled "Play Next" stack separate from the main queue, plus favorites and back-skip history.

This .ipa is unsigned and built straight from the main branch, so it needs to be sideloaded (AltStore, SideStore, LiveContainer, etc.) rather than installed from the App Store.
apps.versionDescription:
- Long song titles scroll instead of being cut off. A title, album or artist wider than the space it has now holds at its start, travels to its end, waits there, and comes back -- in the mini player, in the pill the player shrinks to, and on the Now Playing screen, where all three lines move as one block rather than each drifting at its own pace. Lines that fit still sit still, and with Reduce Motion on nothing moves at all. Long titles are the norm on this screen -- classical movements, remix credits, multi-artist billings -- and it is the screen you opened to read what is playing, so an ellipsis was the wrong answer on any of them.
- The mini player gives the song's name the whole row it was already occupying. The title used to stop a quarter of the way short of the play button with nothing but empty space between, however long it was: the row split its free width evenly between the title and the gap in front of the controls. The title now claims that width itself, and the play and skip buttons sit as one pair against the pill's edge instead of drifting apart with the row's spacing between them.
- The Settings server row no longer carries a blue circle with a music note in it. The row says which server you are on; the badge said nothing the row didn't.

- The Settings server row no longer carries a blue circle with a music note in it. The row says which server you are on; the badge said nothing the row didn't.

- The Now Playing song info line says where the music is coming from in a single word: "Cache" for a copy on the device, "Stream" for one arriving live, in place of the longer "Cached" and "Streaming". Same meaning, less of the line spent on it, so the codec and bitrate beside it stay readable.

- A bad connection no longer ends in silence with no way back. The app now health-checks the connection continuously: a ping and a small timed download against your own server when the app starts, every time it returns to the foreground, and on a rolling interval in between, alongside speed measurements taken off the transfers it is already making -- so a link too slow to stream is known *before* the first song is asked to survive it, not learned from its failure. The moment the link looks unfit -- slow pings, measured speed below what streaming needs, a playback failure or a pair of timeouts -- it stops handing the player live streams that can't survive it, and the verdict is remembered across launches. On a connection judged bad, each song is downloaded ahead of playing: the buffering indicator sits in the Now Playing screen's year-and-genre line, the download fills the seek bar as a faint pulsing layer behind the playhead, and the music starts once a third of the song is on the device -- the rest keeps downloading underneath while it plays. If playback catches up with the download, it pauses and shows buffering again until the file is comfortably ahead, with the play button held (no timeout -- skipping always works) whenever sound is held. The download retries on its own for as long as you leave the song waiting -- and every failed attempt immediately asks the next one for a lower bitrate, down to an emergency floor below anything Settings offers, because on a link that bad the smaller song is the one that arrives. The song info line reads "Loading" for the whole transfer and names the codec and bitrate actually being fetched -- not the Settings choice -- keeps naming them for the rest of the listen, and flips to "Cached" (never "Streaming") once the download completes mid-song. Downloads use the system's background transfer service where the install supports it (so they keep running while the app is suspended), fall back to in-process transfers where it doesn't -- sideloaded installs mostly don't -- and remember the answer, with the in-process path keeping going for a stretch after backgrounding and picking straight back up when you return. And recovery is deliberately hard to earn: a bad-connection verdict stands for at least three minutes however fast the bursts look, fast transfers only count once the link has gone two minutes without an actual failure, and a link that merely limps along keeps the verdict alive instead of quietly aging out of it -- so the *next* song on a still-bad connection is preloaded too, rather than handed to a stream that dies. The quality setting is treated as a target rather than a promise: a struggling link is asked for a bitrate it can actually carry -- stepped down as far as needed, judged from the measured speed -- and the smaller copy is upgraded automatically the next time the song plays on a healthy connection, the same way lesser cached copies always have been. A stream that dies mid-song recovers by itself, a downloaded copy that refuses to play is thrown away and fetched afresh instead of failing on every press, and the play button sits out the first stretch of a buffering wait -- dimmed, coming back after half a minute regardless. Songs already on the device play on a bad connection whatever quality they were saved at. Once songs move at full speed again, the app goes back to ordinary streaming by itself.
- On a bad connection the songs come first, the pictures after. While the current song -- and then the next ones, which keep prefetching on a bad connection precisely because the song playing is already on the device -- are being downloaded, cover art, lock-screen artwork and the queue's "more like this" lookups hold off rather than competing for a link that can barely carry one thing, and catch up the moment the songs are through. The rare playback error that still surfaces now speaks your language properly instead of quoting the system's one-line apology.
- The log now says what actually went wrong, and says it in English. A failure used to be written down as the one-line apology iOS composes in the device's language — "Vorgang kann nicht abgeschlossen werden", which names neither the operation nor why it couldn't be — while the error's real content, the code and the chain of causes underneath it, was thrown away. A playback failure on a bad connection now reads like "the operation could not be completed (AVErrorUnknown, see the underlying error) [AVFoundationErrorDomain -11800] -- caused by: the network connection was lost mid-transfer [NSURLErrorDomain -1005]", whatever language the phone is set to. Error banners in the app itself are unchanged and still speak your language; this is about the log you read and export under Settings → Diagnostics.

- Songs you listen to are kept, without being downloaded a second time. A song that wasn't already on the device used to be fetched twice over: once to play it, and once again, from the same server, to keep it — two transcodes of one song, racing each other. It cost enough that it was only ever done on Wi-Fi, so nothing you played on cellular was kept at all. The bytes that play the song are now written down as they arrive, so keeping it costs nothing beyond hearing it, and it happens on every connection.
- Songs stop breaking up mid-play and restarting from the beginning. When a stream stalled, iOS asked the server for it again — and a server transcoding as it sends can only answer by starting the song over, which was heard as the track jumping back to its beginning while the progress bar carried on regardless, every position wrong from then on. What has already arrived is now held on the device, so that second ask is answered from there instead of from the server.
- A song is only kept when the whole of it arrived. Skipping part way through, or scrubbing, leaves nothing behind rather than a partial file — a half-finished song still claims its full length, and once kept it would play out early or scrub to the wrong place every time. Nothing kept this way skips the checks a download goes through: it is verified against the length the server reports, and repacked so scrubbing lands exactly.

- Settings no longer says the version twice. The footer read "SwiftDrome 0.8.1 (0.8.1)" — the brackets are where iOS puts the build number, and there was nothing to put in them, so they only repeated what stood in front of them. The commit the build came from now sits there instead, on the same line rather than a line of its own: "SwiftDrome 0.8.2 (a1b2c3d)", or "(local)" for a build made on your own machine. The line is still selectable, to be pasted into a bug report.

- The logs can be read in the app. Settings → Diagnostics used to offer one thing, an export, which meant diagnosing anything on the device started by sending files to another app. That row now leads to the log itself: newest entries first, filterable by category and down to errors only, and searchable by text. A crash or a hang report sits at the top of the screen when there is one, and opens as the text it is. The export is still there, on the same screen, and still hands over everything — what you filtered the view down to never changes what gets sent.
- Rows that lead somewhere answer anywhere along them. Logs in Settings, and Playlists, Artists, Albums and the rest of the Library list, only reacted where something was drawn — the words and the chevron — so a tap in the space between them, or just above or below the text, did nothing at all. The whole row is the target now.
- Settings says which build is installed. Every preview build of a pull request carries the last release's version number, so two of them were indistinguishable once installed; the footer now shows the commit each build came from underneath the version, and reads "local" for a build made on your own machine. The line can be selected and copied straight into a bug report.

- Songs streamed as Opus can be downloaded again. Every Opus download was being thrown away the moment it finished, on the grounds that it had arrived incomplete — and it hadn't: iOS works an Opus file's length out from an assumed bitrate rather than reading the length the file states, and it was wrong by up to half a minute on a three-and-a-half-minute song. Nothing reached the device, so nothing could be played offline, and the app kept trying: the same song was fetched again a second later, and again, for as long as it was in the queue. An Opus file is now measured by what it says about itself, exact to the sample, and the check that rejects a genuinely truncated download is the file's own account of whether it ended.
- Scrubbing a song streamed as Opus now lands where you drop it. A server transcodes as it sends, so the stream has no length and no way to be asked for a position part way through — a scrub either settled back where playback already was or never arrived. The app now asks the server to start the song where you dropped the scrubber, which it can do because it is reading its own file, and covers the last fraction of a second itself. Landing is exact. Servers that don't support this are detected rather than assumed, and scrubbing behaves as it did before on them.
- The length shown for an Opus song is the song's, not an estimate. The progress bar could be built on a length several percent short of the audio — a three-minute song reported as two-fifty — which put every position, the remaining time and the end of the track out with it.
- A download that fails is no longer retried immediately, over and over. One that couldn't be fetched was being started again the instant it failed, roughly once a second for as long as the song stayed in the queue, and each attempt pulled the whole song down before being discarded. A failed download now waits five minutes, and the songs behind it in the queue are fetched in the meantime instead of being held up behind it.
- Scrubbing a lossless song now lands where you drop it. Dragging to 2:50 in a three-minute FLAC could start the audio nearly a minute earlier while the progress bar and the remaining time both insisted you were where you had asked to be — iOS works a FLAC's position out from an assumed bitrate instead of reading the seek table the file carries, so the further into a song you reached the further short it landed, and it reported the position you asked for either way. Downloaded songs are now kept in a container iOS can seek exactly: still lossless, still the same audio, and about the same size on disk. A song that is still streaming is fetched from the byte your seek points at, which lands within a tenth of a second. Nothing on the server is touched, re-encoded or renamed — this happens on the device, to the app's own copy.
- Reopening the app returns to where you left a lossless song, rather than to wherever the seek happened to land. The check meant to catch a restored position that missed was trusting a clock that reports the position it was asked for, so it never found anything to correct.
- A download that arrives incomplete no longer becomes a permanently broken song. Two ways a bad file used to end up in the cache looking like a good one: a server answering with an error page instead of the track, stored as if it were music, and a connection closing part-way through a transfer the app had no length to check it against. Either one is poison once cached — a half-finished FLAC still claims the full length in its header, so it plays out early, skips, or lands somewhere else every time you scrub. Downloads are now checked against the file size and length the server reports for the track, and anything short is discarded instead of kept.
- The app has a real icon. Installed builds used to sit on the home screen as a blank placeholder, because nothing in the build carried an icon at all; SwiftDrome now ships its own mark — two triangles for the outgoing and incoming track, with the overlap where both are audible drawn in its own lighter colour. The same mark greets you on the login screen in place of the stock music symbol, and the AltStore source now shows it as the app's icon and header rather than two broken images.

- The app can be installed and updated from the AltStore source again. Every build so far reported itself as version 1.0.0 no matter which release it was — the version was never written into the app, so the build tool filled in its own placeholder — and AltStore refuses to install an app whose version disagrees with the one the source advertises. Builds now carry their real version number, and the source lists the iOS version the app actually needs (26) rather than the 17 it was seeded with.
